claims.text: Untreated Q235 steel has a thin, naturally formed iron oxide film in its pre-exposure state.
The native iron oxide film provides effective corrosion protection to Q235 steel at room temperature.
Exposure to aggressive salt at 700–900 °C causes the native oxide on Q235 steel to crack and spall.
Thermal stresses and accelerated oxidation are the causes of oxide cracking and spallation at 700–900 °C.
Breakdown of the oxide exposes underlying Q235 steel and accelerates corrosion.
As-received Q235 steel contains inherent microstructural heterogeneities.
Room-temperature and 700–900 °C exposures should use identical salt compositions and exposure durations.
The room-temperature salt condition constitutes mild oxidation under which the native oxide remains intact.
High temperature accelerates oxidation kinetics and imposes thermal-expansion stresses on the oxide.
The integrity, continuity, and adhesion of the native iron oxide film govern corrosion protection.
An intact native oxide limits ion transport and corrosion at room temperature.
Differential thermal expansion between the oxide and Q235 steel leads to oxide cracking and spallation.
Loss of oxide integrity reduces passivation and exposes fresh metal to corrosive attack.
Q235 steel exposed to aggressive salt at room temperature will exhibit minimal mass change and a low corrosion rate.
Q235 steel exposed to aggressive salt at 700–900 °C will exhibit oxide breakdown, greater mass loss, and enhanced corrosion indicators relative to room-temperature exposure.
The native oxide remains stable when as-received Q235 steel is kept in a non-aggressive or inert environment.
The proposed mechanism is limited to untreated Q235 steel without protective coatings or alloying modifications.
Alternative stabilization of the oxide could prevent the proposed high-temperature failure mechanism.
